description: Tar Solo: one human plus one AI. Claude Code is my AI co-pilot for code, physics and research. We build Mission: Mars, a browser game on NASA data (JPL Horizons, DSN, SOA 2026) that teaches mission design from school level to engineer level. Join us if you love space education, game design or orbital mechanics. Wanted: a UX/visual designer and an aerospace engineer or science teacher to check the facts.
summary: Mission: Mars is a browser game that lets anyone design a small spacecraft, launch it to Mars and see whether it makes it. It answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge with four levels of difficulty: Rookie and Explorer for school students, Student for university level, and Engineer for professionals. The player chooses instruments, fuel, launch date, rocket, engine, solar panels, radio band and orbit, while a live forecast shows what works and why. The physics runs on real NASA data: planet positions from JPL Horizons, small-spacecraft technology from the NASA State of the Art report, radio blackout limits from NASA ASCEND, and Deep Space Network antenna data. Random events such as navigation errors and dust storms teach why engineers keep margins. Every number is marked as real data or game design, and every term has a "?" explanation with sources. It matters because mission design is usually hidden behind equations; here learners see trade-offs between mass, fuel, power, data and cost, and finish by comparing their design with real NASA missions.
details:
Play online, no installation or account: https://z-shark.github.io/mission-mars/ (source code and documentation: https://github.com/z-shark/mission-mars)

What it does

Mission: Mars is a single-player web game about designing a Mars mission. The player reads a letter from scientists, chooses what to take and how much fuel to carry, picks a launch date, and presses Launch. A live forecast panel recalculates after every change and says what is red, what is green and what to change. After the flight the game shows a report with the numbers, explains what held the design back, and compares it with real NASA Mars missions (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and MAVEN).

Four levels

Rookie: three simple steps with instruments and fuel. Explorer: free launch date, solar panels, observation time and a credit budget. Student: rocket, engine, radio band and a list of requirements to meet. Engineer: no pictures, a requirement matrix, orbit shape, radio antenna and transmitter, sensitivity analysis, a Monte Carlo of 500 random flights, a full link budget, a table of assumptions with sources, and JSON and CSV export. There are 16 missions across the levels, each with a "You will learn" line before the flight and a takeaway after it.

How it works

The transfer between Earth and Mars is solved as Lambert's problem between real positions of the planets from NASA JPL Horizons. The rocket equation uses engine data from the NASA State of the Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report. Capture into an elliptical orbit, orbit period (Kepler), solar power at Mars, radio delay and solar conjunction blackout (angles from NASA ASCEND 2022) are calculated from the same data. At the Engineer level the radio link is computed with the receive gain and noise temperature of a 34 m Deep Space Network antenna from the NASA DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook. Dice rolls for a navigation surprise and a dust storm show why engineers carry margins; the same design can end differently, and an optional random seed repeats a flight.

Real data and game design are kept apart

Values with a source live in one data file and game-design values (masses and costs of the game spacecraft, budgets, requirement thresholds, probabilities of random events) in another. The game says so in a "What is real, and what is game design?" popup and in every "?" term explanation, which has three levels of detail (Simple, More detail, Student), a Real data line, a Game design line and source links. Known limits are stated openly: launch vehicle limits are upper bounds, no public launch-energy curve exists for the small rocket, and credits are not money.

Benefits and intended impact

Learners see why a Mars mission is a set of trade-offs between mass, fuel, power, data and cost, not just a formula. The same engine serves school students and adults, so a learner can move up level by level. The game is free, needs no installation, no account and no build step, and runs from static files, so a teacher can open it from a link or from a downloaded folder.

Tools

Plain JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS with no framework, inline SVG for charts and diagrams, Node.js built-in test runner (51 automated tests for physics, the transfer solver and the game model), Python scripts for downloading and preparing NASA data, Git and GitHub Pages for hosting.

What is creative

The four-level design that reuses one physics model; the visible split between real data and game design; the Engineer level that turns the game into a small design-review tool (requirements, Monte Carlo, link budget, sensitivity, export); and honest randomness that is explained instead of hidden.

Factors considered

Accuracy over spectacle: every number has a recorded source with a direct link. Accessibility for different ages: the same screen explains terms at three depths. The text is kept in a separate file so a Ukrainian translation can be added later.

Team and use of AI

Claude Code (Anthropic) helped write the game code. The author chose the physics, the data and the sources, and checked every formula and every source link. AI did not generate any NASA data: all NASA numbers come from the cited documents. AI also helped draft the text of this page and the presentation, and the author edited it. The team photo at the top of this page is an AI-generated image, made with Easy Diffusion.

Source code and documentation: https://github.com/z-shark/mission-mars
